new_statements.translation: 2.1.2. There is no stress in Looma. Two level phonetic tones are contrasted, low and high: pà 'to come', pá 'to kill'. The bearer of phonetic tone is the syllable. The segmental bearer of phonological tone, i.e. of the toneme, is the morpheme. A toneme may be represented by one phonetic tone or by a sequence of tones; in the latter case the morpheme may have a level or a gliding contour.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Looma (Guinean Woi-Balagha dialect) is described as having no word stress at all; word prosody is tonal, with two level tones (H, L) carried by syllables and tonemes assigned per morpheme, lexemes grouped into tonal classes.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Only a special intonation contour for imperative/interrogative sentences is mentioned elsewhere (phrase-level intonation, not stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the word-prosodic system of the language as a whole (Jazyki mira template slot 2.1.2 'stress'); data explicitly from the Guinean Woi-Balagha dialect, the basis of the Guinean literary norm. For the Liberian variety (loma1260) Dwyer 1981 says only 'Lorma is a syllable-timed language' and gives a generic Mande/Kpelle stress remark, no Lorma-specific placement.
new_statements.identity_note: Mishchenko 2017 describes 'Looma' as one language spoken in Guinea and Liberia, but states (sec. 2.0.0) that the description rests on her own field data from the Guinean Woi-Balagha dialect (Macenta prefecture), the basis of the Guinean literary norm -- i.e. Glottolog's Toma (toma1245), under which Glottolog itself files this chapter. The other files saved (Vydrine 1989, Dwyer 1981 x2) describe Liberian Loma/Lorma dialects (Gizima, Ziema, Bulima, Gbunde) = loma1260 and contain no Loma-specific stress placement (Dwyer: 'syllable-timed', two tones).

sources.note: Sec. 2.1.2: 'Ударение в Л.я. отсутствует.' (There is no stress in Looma.) Then: two level tones (low, high); phonetic tone-bearing unit is the syllable; the toneme's segmental domain is the morpheme; nouns fall into 7 tonal classes. Description explicitly based on the Guinean Woi-Balagha dialect from the author's fieldwork (sec. 2.0.0).

sources.citation: Dwyer, David J. and Bodegie, P. and Bague, J. D. (1981). A learner directed approach to Lorma: a handbook on communication and culture with dialogs, texts, cultural notes, exercises, drills, and instructions. East Lansing: African Studies Center, Michigan State University. 355 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: The handbook explicitly describes the Zorzor variety of Liberian Lorma (Introduction sec. 5 'Dialects', ERIC PDF p. 15: 'This book was written (as requested) using the Zorzor variety of Lorma'), i.e. Glottolog loma1260, not the Guinean Woi-Balagha dialect (toma1245) the catalog record and Mishchenko 2017 describe. It is also silent on word stress, so it neither confirms nor contradicts Mishchenko's 'Ударение в Л.я. отсутствует'; it is compatible in that both describe a two-level-tone language (H/L).

sources.note: Sec. 3.35: 'Lorma is a syllable-timed language.' Mande-family appendix: 'While stress is generally non-contrastive in Mande it is generally distinctive. In Kpelle, it falls on the first high-toned syllable in the word, or if the word has no high tones, it falls on the first syllable.' -- a generic Mande/Kpelle statement, no Lorma-specific stress placement; Lorma has two tones; rising/falling contours only as sentence intonation.
